adversarial_test_results.prompt: Marcus inherited boxes of unsorted letters when his grandmother died, and he promised himself he would read them all before the house sold. The attic smelled of cedar and dust. He carried the first box downstairs and set it beside the armchair. Night after night he opened envelopes, smoothed the paper flat, and stacked pages in neat piles. Some letters described harvests and weddings. Others listed debts and repairs. A few contained only recipes for bread and soup. He learned names of cousins he had never met and traced old feuds nobody discussed anymore. His sister called twice to ask about his progress, and he told her the boxes seemed endless. One winter night a pipe burst and soaked two folders, so he dried each sheet with towels and copied the blurred lines onto fresh paper. The work felt slow, yet he kept going because each bundle taught him something new. Friends stopped visiting after he declined every invitation for a month. He brewed coffee, sharpened pencils, and kept long lists of dates and questions in a notebook. He taped a map to the wall and pinned each letter to the town it came from. Slowly a picture of three generations emerged from the fragments. When spring arrived, only one box remained unopened. He lifted the lid and studied the bundled envelopes wrapped in brown paper and string. His hands shook a little as he realized the task would soon end. He cleared the table, poured one last cup of coffee, and settled into the chair where this whole project had started so many months earlier. On the last evening he sat down, opened the final bundle, and read through the entire manuscript in a single sitting.
